messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Akash, a 29-year-old South Asian man married to his college sweetheart, has been struggling with intrusive memories and intense reactions following a mugging that occurred six months ago. The event happened while he was returning home late one night after working long hours as a painter. A masked assailant suddenly appeared behind him, demanding his wallet and phone at gunpoint. Akash froze in fear, barely registering the commands until he felt a sharp pain on his arm where he had been cut by the attacker during the struggle. The trauma has left deep scars both physically and mentally. He wakes up almost every night from nightmares of that moment, feeling the cold metal of the gun pressed against him and seeing the masked face looming over him. These nightmares often trigger waking moments filled with a sense of dread, especially when he visits locations similar to where the mugging took place. The tension in his body is palpable as he walks through these areas, constantly scanning for any signs of danger. Akash’s irritability has become a defining feature of his life post-trauma. He often lashes out at his wife and colleagues over minor issues, driven by an underlying fear that he cannot fully explain or control. The memory of the mugging is fragmented; when he tries to recall the event deliberately, it feels like pieces are missing. This incomplete picture contributes to a sense of unreality about what happened, making it difficult for him to process and integrate his experience. The guilt he feels during these memories compounds his distress. He wonders if he could have done more to avoid being hurt or whether his hesitation somehow made the situation worse. The difficulty in recalling details only adds to this guilt, as he cannot fully piece together the sequence of events that led to his injury. Akash has become increasingly mistrustful and isolated since the incident. His belief that people can’t be trusted is reinforced by every trigger, each time making him feel more set apart from others. He finds it hard to rely on anyone, believing they might not understand or could potentially put him in danger again. This mistrust fuels his constant sense of threat, causing his body to remain perpetually tense and ready to react at any moment. The triggers themselves have become a vicious cycle. Every time he wakes up from a nightmare or revisits the location where it happened, the memories flood back with intense guilt and a sense of helplessness. This rekindles the belief that he can’t trust anyone, making him more vigilant and suspicious. His body stays on high alert, scanning for danger continuously. This cycle has taken a toll on Akash’s work as well. He finds it difficult to focus on painting projects and often misses deadlines due to his distracted state. His irritability at the job site sometimes leads to conflicts with colleagues, further isolating him from others both personally and professionally. What finally brought Akash to seek help was a particularly bad episode where he had an angry outburst at work, leading to a reprimand from his supervisor. He realizes that if things continue this way, his marriage and career could suffer irreparably. Despite his mistrust of others, the fear of losing everything is overwhelming him, making him hopeful that therapy might provide some relief from this relentless cycle of anxiety and guilt.
